title: Understanding the Problem Before Designing the Solution
objectives: Recognise and avoid premature solutioning in architecture work
Apply structured problem framing techniques to ambiguous briefs
Understand how discovery works in UK government and why it matters
Distinguish the real problem from the stated problem
Connect policy intent to technical problem definition
whyThisMatters:
The single most expensive mistake in solution architecture is solving the wrong problem. It happens constantly in government: a policy team asks for a database, when what they actually need is a reporting capability. A programme board approves a platform rebuild when the real issue is a broken process. A delivery team builds a sophisticated workflow engine when a spreadsheet would have done. Every one of these failures started with an architect who jumped to designing before they understood the problem.

In UK government, the cost of premature solutioning is amplified. Public money is spent. Procurement cycles are long. Political timelines are unforgiving. If you build the wrong thing, you can't just pivot like a startup — you're locked into contracts, committed to delivery dates announced by ministers, and accountable to Parliament. Discovery exists precisely to prevent this. As a Solution Architect, your ability to hold the space for genuine problem understanding — resisting the pressure to start designing — is one of the most valuable things you bring.

content.heading: The Danger of Premature Solutioning
content.body:
Premature solutioning is the occupational hazard of every technically minded person. Someone describes a problem, and before they've finished the second sentence, your brain is already sketching a solution. It feels productive. It feels like you're adding value. It's almost always a mistake.

Here's why. When you solution early, you anchor on the first framing of the problem you hear. That framing is almost never the right one. The person describing the problem is describing their experience of it — their symptoms, their frustrations, their assumptions about what would fix it. They're not describing the root cause, the full context, or the range of people affected.

Consider a real pattern that plays out in government regularly. A policy team comes to you and says: 'We need a database to track energy performance certificates.' What they actually need is the ability to answer questions like 'How many commercial buildings in the North East have an EPC rating below C?' They've jumped from their need (answering questions about energy performance) to a solution (a database) without considering whether the data already exists somewhere, whether an existing analytical tool could answer their questions, or whether the real problem is data quality rather than data storage.

If you accept their framing and start designing a database, you'll build something that technically works but doesn't solve the real problem. You'll have spent public money on a solution that either duplicates existing capability or addresses a symptom rather than a cause.

The antidote is discipline. When someone presents you with a solution request, your first job is to work backwards to the problem. Ask: 'What are you trying to achieve?' not 'What do you want me to build?' Ask: 'What happens today?' not 'What should the system do?' Ask: 'Who needs this and why?' not 'What are the requirements?'

This isn't about being difficult or slowing things down. It's about ensuring that the significant investment of time, money, and effort that follows is directed at the right target. In government, where changing direction mid-project is extraordinarily expensive, getting the problem right is the highest-value activity an architect can perform.

content.heading: Problem Framing Techniques That Actually Work
content.body:
Problem framing is a skill, not an instinct. Here are the techniques that work consistently in government architecture contexts.

**The Problem Statement Canvas:** Write a single statement that captures: Who is affected? What is the problem they experience? What is the impact? What evidence do we have? A good problem statement for the EPC example might be: 'Policy analysts in DESNZ (who) cannot reliably determine the energy performance profile of commercial buildings by region (problem) which means they cannot target retrofit incentive programmes effectively (impact), evidenced by the three-month delay in producing the 2023 regional analysis (evidence).'

Notice what this does. It shifts the conversation from 'build us a database' to 'help us answer questions about energy performance by region.' The solution space is now much wider — it might be a database, but it might also be better access to existing data, a reporting tool on top of existing systems, or even a process change.

**The Five Whys (Government Edition):** The classic Five Whys technique works well in government, but you need to adapt it. In a commercial setting, you can usually trace problems to operational root causes. In government, the root cause is often a policy decision, an organisational boundary, or a legacy procurement choice. Be prepared to follow the chain into uncomfortable territory.

Why can't the policy team answer regional EPC questions? Because the data is in three different systems. Why is it in three different systems? Because three different programmes collected it at different times. Why were there three different programmes? Because the policy changed twice and each iteration created a new data collection mechanism without decommissioning the old one. Why wasn't the old mechanism decommissioned? Because nobody owned the data lifecycle. Now you're at the real problem — data governance, not data storage.

**Context Mapping:** Before you can frame the problem properly, you need to understand the landscape. Draw a simple map showing: the users and their needs, the existing systems and data sources, the organisational boundaries, the policy drivers, and the constraints. This doesn't need to be a formal architecture diagram — a whiteboard sketch is fine. The point is to make the context visible so you can see where the real problem sits.

**Assumption Surfacing:** Every brief comes loaded with assumptions. Your job is to surface them and test them. When someone says 'we need real-time data,' ask what 'real-time' means to them — it might mean 'within 24 hours' rather than 'sub-second.' When someone says 'all users need access,' ask who the users actually are — it might be twelve people, not twelve thousand. When someone says 'it must integrate with System X,' ask why — the integration might be a workaround for a problem that could be solved differently.

Each surfaced assumption either confirms a constraint (which is useful) or reveals a false constraint (which is even more useful, because it opens up the solution space).

content.heading: Discovery in Government: What It Is and Why Architects Must Engage
content.body:
The GDS Service Manual defines discovery as the phase where you learn about the problem you're trying to solve. It's not optional. It's not a formality. It's the foundation on which everything else is built.

In practice, discovery in government involves:

**User research:** Understanding who the users are, what they need, and how they currently meet those needs (or fail to). As an SA, you're not conducting the user research yourself — that's the user researcher's job — but you must engage with the findings. User research reveals constraints and requirements that no amount of technical analysis will uncover. If users are currently working around a system's limitations with spreadsheets and phone calls, that tells you something important about what the solution needs to do.

**Stakeholder engagement:** Identifying everyone who has a stake in the outcome and understanding their perspectives. In government, this always includes more people than you initially think. Policy teams, operational teams, legal advisors, data protection officers, security teams, commercial teams, GDS assessors, and sometimes ministers' private offices all have legitimate interests that shape the problem.

**Landscape analysis:** Understanding what already exists. What systems are in place? What data is available? What services could be reused? What contracts constrain your options? In government, the landscape is often more complex than anyone realises, because systems have accumulated over decades and institutional knowledge has been lost as people move on.

**Constraint identification:** Mapping the hard constraints (legal requirements, security classifications, accessibility standards, procurement rules) and soft constraints (budget, timeline, team capability, political priorities). Hard constraints define the boundaries of your solution space. Soft constraints shape the trade-offs you'll need to make.

As a Solution Architect, your role in discovery is specific and critical. You're not there to design the solution — that comes later. You're there to ensure that the problem is understood well enough that a good solution can be designed. You bring the technical perspective that helps the team understand what's feasible, what's complex, and what questions need answering before design can begin.

The most common failure mode for architects in discovery is impatience. You see the problem, you see a solution, and you want to start building. Resist this. Discovery is where you earn the right to design well. Skip it, and you'll pay for it later — in rework, in missed requirements, in solutions that don't fit the real problem.

content.heading: Understanding Policy Intent: The Hidden Driver
content.body:
In government, every digital service exists to implement policy. This is a fundamental difference from the private sector, where services exist to generate revenue or reduce costs. If you don't understand the policy intent behind a service, you can't design it well.

Policy intent is the 'why behind the why.' The policy team wants to collect energy performance data (the stated need) because the government has committed to achieving net zero by 2050 and needs to understand the current state of building energy efficiency to target interventions effectively (the policy intent). Understanding this deeper intent changes how you approach the architecture.

If you only know 'collect energy performance data,' you might design a simple data collection form. If you understand the policy intent, you realise the data needs to be analytically useful, comparable across regions and time periods, linkable to other datasets (building ownership, retrofit grants, planning applications), and accessible to multiple teams across government. The architecture implications are fundamentally different.

How do you uncover policy intent? Ask these questions:

- What legislation or ministerial commitment drives this work?
- What outcome is the policy trying to achieve?
- How will success be measured?
- What decisions will be made using the data or service outputs?
- How might the policy evolve over the next 3-5 years?
- Are there related policies in other departments that this needs to align with?

The last two questions are particularly important. Government policy evolves constantly. A service designed for today's policy that can't adapt to tomorrow's policy change is a service that will need replacing sooner than anyone wants. Understanding the direction of policy travel helps you make architecture decisions that are resilient to change.

Policy teams don't always articulate their intent clearly — not because they're being difficult, but because they think in policy terms, not technical terms. Your job as an SA is to translate between these worlds. When a policy colleague says 'we need to incentivise building owners to improve energy efficiency,' you need to hear the architecture implications: data collection, eligibility checking, payment processing, compliance monitoring, reporting, and audit.

content.heading: The Real Problem vs the Stated Problem
content.body:
Every experienced architect has a collection of stories where the stated problem and the real problem were completely different. Developing the skill to distinguish between them is essential.

The stated problem is what you're told. 'We need a new case management system.' 'The database is too slow.' 'We need to migrate to the cloud.' 'We need an API for this data.'

The real problem is what's actually causing pain. The case management system isn't the problem — the problem is that three teams are using three different processes and can't see each other's work. The database isn't slow — the queries are inefficient because the data model doesn't match how the data is actually used. The cloud migration isn't needed for technical reasons — it's needed because the data centre contract is expiring. The API isn't needed for integration — it's needed because a specific team can't access data they need and an API is the only solution they can think of.

How do you find the real problem? Three approaches work consistently:

**Follow the pain.** Ask people what frustrates them about the current situation. Not what they want the new system to do — what's wrong with how things work today. The answers will point you toward the real problem. If everyone complains about the same thing, that's your signal.

**Observe the workarounds.** People are creative. When a system doesn't meet their needs, they build workarounds — spreadsheets, email chains, manual processes, shadow IT. These workarounds are gold for an architect because they show you what the system should do but doesn't. Map the workarounds and you've mapped the gap between the stated problem and the real one.

**Challenge the brief.** This requires courage, especially in government where hierarchy matters. But a good SA challenges the brief respectfully. 'You've asked for a new case management system. Before we design one, can I spend a week understanding why the current one isn't working? It might be that we can fix the current system for a fraction of the cost.' This isn't being obstructive — it's being responsible with public money.

The real problem is often less glamorous than the stated one. Nobody wants to hear that their exciting platform rebuild could be avoided by fixing a data quality issue and training staff on the existing system. But if that's the truth, it's your job to say it. The best architects save their organisations from expensive solutions to cheap problems.

content.heading: Structured Approaches to Problem Analysis
content.body:
Beyond the techniques already discussed, several structured approaches help you analyse problems systematically.

**Impact Mapping:** Start with the goal (what outcome are we trying to achieve?), then identify the actors (who can help or hinder?), then the impacts (what behaviours need to change?), and finally the deliverables (what could we build or do to create those impacts?). This keeps the focus on outcomes rather than outputs and prevents the common trap of building features that don't contribute to the goal.

For a DESNZ energy reporting service, the impact map might look like: Goal: 'Accurate regional energy performance data available within 48 hours of collection.' Actors: building owners (submit data), DESNZ analysts (use data), local authorities (enforce compliance). Impacts: building owners submit accurate data on time, analysts can query data by region and building type. Deliverables: online submission service, validation engine, analytical dashboard.

**Wardley Mapping:** Simon Wardley's mapping technique is particularly useful in government because it helps you understand the maturity of different components and make appropriate build/buy/reuse decisions. Plot the components of your problem space on a map from genesis (novel, uncertain) to commodity (well-understood, standardised). Components that are commodities should be bought or reused. Components that are novel might need custom development. This prevents the common government mistake of building custom solutions for commodity problems.

**PESTLE for Architecture:** Adapt the classic PESTLE analysis (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, Environmental) for architecture problem analysis. Political: what ministerial priorities or cross-departmental dynamics affect this? Economic: what budget constraints and value-for-money requirements apply? Social: what user needs and accessibility requirements exist? Technological: what existing systems, platforms, and capabilities are available? Legal: what legislation, data protection requirements, and regulatory constraints apply? Environmental: what sustainability considerations matter?

**Cynefin Framework:** Dave Snowden's Cynefin framework helps you understand what kind of problem you're dealing with. Is it obvious (clear cause and effect, apply best practice)? Complicated (cause and effect discoverable with expertise, apply good practice)? Complex (cause and effect only visible in retrospect, probe and respond)? Chaotic (no clear cause and effect, act and stabilise)? Most government architecture problems are complicated or complex. Treating a complex problem as if it were merely complicated — applying a standard pattern without experimentation — is a recipe for failure.

The key insight across all these approaches: they're tools for thinking, not bureaucratic exercises. Use them to structure your analysis and challenge your assumptions. Don't use them to produce impressive-looking documents that nobody reads. A problem well-understood on a whiteboard is worth more than a problem poorly understood in a 50-page report.

content.heading: When Discovery Goes Wrong: Patterns of Failure
content.body:
Understanding how discovery fails helps you avoid the traps.

**The Confirmation Bias Trap:** You go into discovery with a solution already in mind and unconsciously seek evidence that supports it. Every piece of user research that aligns with your preconception gets highlighted; everything that contradicts it gets explained away. The antidote is to actively seek disconfirming evidence. Ask yourself: 'What would I need to see to abandon my current hypothesis?'

**The Stakeholder Capture Trap:** The loudest or most senior stakeholder dominates the problem definition. Their view of the problem becomes the team's view, even if it's partial or wrong. In government, this often manifests as the policy team's framing going unchallenged because they're seen as the 'customer.' The antidote is to ensure you hear from all stakeholders, especially the operational staff who deal with the problem daily and the end users who experience it.

**The Scope Creep Trap:** Discovery reveals that the problem is bigger than anyone thought. Instead of narrowing the focus to something achievable, the team tries to solve everything at once. The antidote is ruthless prioritisation. What is the minimum problem we need to solve first? What can wait for a later phase?

**The Analysis Paralysis Trap:** The team becomes so committed to understanding the problem perfectly that they never move to designing a solution. Discovery becomes an end in itself. The antidote is timeboxing. Set a clear end date for discovery and commit to making decisions with the information you have, accepting that some uncertainty will remain.

**The Technology Hammer Trap:** The team has recently adopted a new technology (Kubernetes, event sourcing, blockchain, AI) and sees every problem as an opportunity to use it. The problem gets reframed to fit the technology rather than the technology being chosen to fit the problem. The antidote is to keep technology choices out of discovery entirely. Focus on the problem and the users. Technology selection comes later.

Recognising these patterns in yourself and your team is a mark of maturity. Every architect falls into these traps occasionally. The good ones notice quickly and correct course.

content.heading: From Problem Understanding to Architecture Readiness
content.body:
Discovery doesn't produce an architecture. It produces the understanding that makes good architecture possible. The bridge between discovery and design is what we might call 'architecture readiness' — the point at which you know enough to start making defensible design decisions.

You're architecture-ready when you can answer these questions:

1. **What problem are we solving and for whom?** You can state this in one or two sentences without using technical jargon.
2. **What does success look like?** You know the measurable outcomes the service needs to achieve.
3. **What are the hard constraints?** You've identified the non-negotiable boundaries — legal, security, accessibility, political.
4. **What already exists?** You've mapped the current landscape — systems, data, services, contracts.
5. **What are the key risks?** You've identified the things that could derail the solution and assessed their likelihood and impact.
6. **Who are the stakeholders and what do they need?** You've mapped the people who matter and understand their perspectives.
7. **What don't we know?** You've identified the remaining uncertainties and have a plan for resolving them.

If you can't answer these questions, you're not ready to design. Going ahead anyway is premature solutioning dressed up as progress.

The output of this phase should be concise and actionable. A good architecture brief — one or two pages that capture the problem, constraints, landscape, risks, and approach — is worth more than a hundred pages of requirements. It gives the team a shared understanding of what they're trying to achieve and why, and it gives you the foundation for making architecture decisions that are grounded in reality rather than assumption.

Remember: the goal of understanding the problem isn't to eliminate all uncertainty. That's impossible. The goal is to reduce uncertainty to the point where you can make reasonable decisions and adapt as you learn more. In government, where the environment is constantly changing — new ministers, new policies, new priorities — the ability to adapt is as important as the ability to plan.

workedExample.title: DESNZ Policy Team's 'Database' Request
workedExample.context: A DESNZ policy team responsible for the Energy Company Obligation (ECO) scheme approaches ICS Digital with a request: 'We need a database to track which energy companies have met their obligations.' They've written a brief that specifies database tables, fields, and even suggests using SQL Server. The request has been approved by their Deputy Director and has a budget allocated. A delivery team is ready to start building.
workedExample.approach:
The Solution Architect resists the temptation to start designing the database and instead spends a week in discovery.

**Day 1-2: Understanding the request.** The SA meets with the policy team and asks: 'Walk me through what you do today and where it breaks down.' It emerges that the team currently receives quarterly spreadsheets from energy companies, manually checks them against obligation targets, and produces a compliance report for the minister. The process takes six weeks each quarter. The 'database' request is really about reducing that six-week cycle.

**Day 3: Following the pain.** The SA observes the team doing their quarterly processing. The bottleneck isn't data storage — it's data validation. Each spreadsheet arrives in a different format, with different interpretations of the data fields. The team spends four of the six weeks cleaning and reconciling data, not querying it.

**Day 4: Mapping the landscape.** The SA discovers that Ofgem already holds much of this data in a structured format as part of their regulatory role. Nobody had thought to check whether the data could be obtained from Ofgem rather than collected directly from energy companies.

**Day 5: Reframing the problem.** The SA presents findings to the policy team: 'Your problem isn't that you lack a database. Your problem is that your data collection process is manual, inconsistent, and duplicates what Ofgem already collects. The solution might be a data feed from Ofgem with automated validation, not a new database.'

**Week 2: Exploring options.** The SA develops three options: (1) Build the database as requested, (2) Establish a data sharing agreement with Ofgem and build a lightweight validation and reporting tool, (3) Improve the spreadsheet templates and build an automated validation tool as an interim measure while pursuing the Ofgem data share.
workedExample.outcome: The programme board selects a combination of Options 2 and 3 — an immediate improvement to the spreadsheet process (reducing the cycle from six weeks to two) while pursuing the Ofgem data share for a longer-term solution. The cost is roughly 40% of the original database proposal, and the outcome is significantly better because it addresses the real problem: data quality and process efficiency, not data storage.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The policy team's request was made in good faith — they genuinely believed a database was the answer. Without the SA's discovery work, a perfectly functional database would have been built that didn't solve the actual problem. The six-week quarterly cycle would have continued because the bottleneck was data quality, not data storage. The SA's value was in asking 'why' before asking 'how,' and in looking beyond the stated request to the underlying need.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Rushed Digital Transformation Brief
civilServiceScenario.background: DESNZ has received a ministerial direction to 'digitise the boiler upgrade scheme application process' within six months. Currently, applications are received by post, processed manually by a team of 30 caseworkers, and decisions are communicated by letter. The minister has seen a demo of a digital service in another department and wants something similar. A programme manager has been appointed and has written a brief calling for 'an online application portal with automated decision-making and real-time status tracking.'
civilServiceScenario.challenge: The brief assumes the solution is a digital portal, but nobody has investigated whether the current process is suitable for digitisation as-is, whether applicants (primarily homeowners and heating installers) want or can use a digital service, or whether the decision-making process can actually be automated. The six-month timeline is extremely aggressive for a service that handles financial payments and has fraud risk.
constraints: Six-month ministerial timeline with high political visibility
Current process involves complex eligibility rules that change frequently
Applicants range from tech-savvy installers to elderly homeowners with limited digital skills
The scheme involves financial payments, requiring robust fraud prevention
Caseworker team has deep process knowledge but limited digital experience
Must meet GDS Service Standard for public-facing services
Existing IT systems are legacy with limited API capability
Budget is fixed and already allocated based on the portal assumption
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect assigned to this programme. The programme manager expects you to start designing the portal immediately. The delivery team is already assembled and billing time.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario tests your ability to push back constructively on premature solutioning while respecting political reality. You can't simply say 'we need six months of discovery' — the minister wants delivery in six months. But you also can't responsibly start building a portal without understanding whether it's the right solution.

The key SA skill here is finding the middle ground: propose a rapid, focused discovery (2-3 weeks) that runs in parallel with early technical work. Use the discovery to validate or challenge the portal assumption while the team sets up the development environment and explores the legacy integration challenges. Frame this not as delay but as risk reduction — 'spending three weeks now to avoid building the wrong thing saves us months of rework later.'

You also need to challenge the automation assumption. Complex eligibility rules that change frequently are notoriously difficult to automate reliably. A hybrid approach — digital application with human decision-making supported by automated checks — might be more realistic and more appropriate for a service involving financial payments.

practiceArtefact.description: Using the boiler upgrade scheme scenario above, produce: (1) A problem statement that reframes the brief from a solution request to a problem definition. (2) A two-week discovery plan that identifies what you need to learn, from whom, and how — while respecting the six-month delivery pressure.
practiceArtefact.guidance: For the problem statement, use the format: Who is affected? What is the problem? What is the impact? What evidence exists? Avoid mentioning any specific technology or solution approach. For the discovery plan, be realistic about what can be achieved in two weeks. Focus on the questions that, if answered wrongly, would lead to the most expensive mistakes. Remember that discovery and early technical work can run in parallel.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Problem Statement:**
Homeowners and heating installers applying for boiler upgrade grants (who) experience a slow, paper-based application process that takes an average of 12 weeks from application to payment (problem), resulting in low scheme uptake, applicant frustration, and inability to meet government retrofit targets (impact). Evidence: scheme uptake is 40% below target, and 23% of applications are abandoned before completion due to process complexity (evidence).

**Two-Week Discovery Plan:**

Week 1 — Understanding Users and Process:
- Days 1-2: Shadow caseworkers processing applications. Map the actual process (not the documented process). Identify where time is spent, where errors occur, and what workarounds exist.
- Day 3: Review a sample of 50 applications to understand data quality, common errors, and rejection reasons.
- Days 4-5: Conduct phone interviews with 8-10 recent applicants (mix of homeowners and installers) to understand their experience and digital capability.

Week 2 — Understanding Constraints and Options:
- Day 6: Meet with the fraud team to understand current fraud patterns and prevention measures.
- Day 7: Assess the legacy systems — what data do they hold, what interfaces exist, what's the realistic integration path?
- Day 8: Meet with the policy team to understand how frequently eligibility rules change and what changes are planned.
- Day 9: Workshop with caseworkers to identify which parts of the process could be digitised immediately and which need human judgment.
- Day 10: Produce discovery findings report with revised problem statement, validated constraints, and recommended approach for alpha.

Parallel technical work during these two weeks: development environment setup, legacy system API assessment, security and data classification review.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about a project where the solution was defined before the problem was fully understood. What happened? What would you do differently now?
How comfortable are you pushing back on a senior stakeholder's solution request to explore the underlying problem? What makes this difficult?
When was the last time you changed your understanding of a problem significantly during discovery? What triggered the change?
How do you currently distinguish between hard constraints (genuinely non-negotiable) and soft constraints (negotiable but presented as fixed)?
What techniques do you use to surface assumptions in a project brief? How effective are they?

knowledgeCheck.question: A policy team asks you to build a database. What should your first response be?
options: Start gathering database requirements — schema, fields, access patterns
Recommend a specific database technology based on the brief
Ask what problem they're trying to solve and what they need to achieve
Explain why databases are not the best solution and suggest alternatives
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Before designing any solution, you need to understand the underlying problem. The request for a 'database' is a solution, not a problem statement. Understanding what the team actually needs to achieve opens up the solution space and prevents premature solutioning.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of the discovery phase in government digital services?
options: To produce a detailed requirements specification for the development team
To learn about the problem you're trying to solve and the users who experience it
To select the technology stack and architecture pattern for the solution
To estimate the cost and timeline for the project
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Discovery is about learning — understanding the problem, the users, the constraints, and the landscape. It's not about producing specifications, choosing technology, or estimating costs, though insights from discovery inform all of these later activities.

knowledgeCheck.question: You discover that the real problem is different from the stated problem. What should you do?
options: Quietly redesign the solution to address the real problem without telling the stakeholders
Present your findings to stakeholders, showing the evidence for the real problem and its implications for the solution approach
Build what was requested — the stakeholders know their business better than you do
Escalate to senior management and refuse to proceed until the brief is corrected
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Transparency is essential. Present your evidence clearly and respectfully, showing stakeholders what you've found and how it changes the picture. This builds trust and leads to better outcomes. Quietly changing direction or blindly following the original brief both carry significant risks.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following is the best indicator that you're ready to move from problem understanding to solution design?
options: The project timeline says discovery is over
You can state the problem in plain language, know the constraints, have mapped the landscape, and have identified the key risks
All stakeholders have signed off on the requirements document
You've completed all the discovery ceremonies recommended by the GDS Service Manual
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architecture readiness is about understanding, not process completion. You're ready to design when you genuinely understand the problem, constraints, landscape, and risks — regardless of whether you've followed every prescribed ceremony or obtained every formal sign-off.

knowledgeCheck.question: A programme board wants to skip discovery because 'we already know what we need.' How should you respond?
options: Accept their decision — they're the programme board and it's their call
Refuse to participate in the programme until discovery is conducted
Propose a rapid, focused discovery that addresses the highest-risk assumptions while respecting the timeline pressure
Document your objection in an email and proceed with design as requested
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The pragmatic approach is to propose a proportionate discovery that addresses the biggest risks. A two-week focused discovery is almost always possible and can prevent months of rework. This respects the board's urgency while fulfilling your professional responsibility to ensure the problem is understood.

practicalExercise.title: Reframing a Solution Request as a Problem Statement
practicalExercise.scenario: You receive the following brief from a DESNZ programme manager: 'We need to build a SharePoint site for the Green Heat Network Fund team. The team currently uses shared drives and email to manage grant applications, assessments, and payments. They want a centralised place to store documents, track application status, and generate reports for the minister. Budget: £150,000. Timeline: 3 months.'
practicalExercise.task:
1. Identify at least 5 assumptions embedded in this brief
2. Write 8 discovery questions you would ask before accepting this brief at face value
3. Rewrite the brief as a problem statement (without mentioning SharePoint or any specific technology)
4. Suggest what a proportionate discovery approach would look like for this request
hints: Consider whether SharePoint is the right tool or just the tool the team knows
Think about what 'manage grant applications' actually involves — is it document storage or workflow?
Consider the reporting requirement — what questions does the minister actually need answered?
Think about whether £150,000 and 3 months is realistic for what's being described
Consider whether there are existing government platforms that handle grant management
practicalExercise.modelAnswer:
**Assumptions in the brief:**
1. SharePoint is the right platform (technology assumption)
2. The problem is about document storage and tracking (problem framing assumption)
3. £150,000 is sufficient budget (cost assumption)
4. 3 months is a realistic timeline (timeline assumption)
5. A single centralised system will meet all needs (scope assumption)
6. The team's current process is correct and just needs digitising (process assumption)
7. Ministerial reporting needs are well understood (requirements assumption)
8. The team has the digital skills to use a new system effectively (capability assumption)

**Discovery Questions:**
1. Walk me through the lifecycle of a grant application from receipt to payment — what happens at each stage and who's involved?
2. What are the biggest pain points in the current process? Where do things go wrong or take too long?
3. How many applications do you process per year, and is this growing?
4. What specific questions does the minister need answered, and how quickly?
5. Have you looked at existing government grant management platforms (e.g., the Government Grants Management Function tools)?
6. What happens when an application is rejected or queried — what's the back-and-forth process?
7. Are there compliance or audit requirements for how grant decisions are recorded and stored?
8. What's the team's experience with SharePoint and other digital tools?

**Reframed Problem Statement:**
The Green Heat Network Fund team (who) manages grant applications, assessments, and payments using fragmented tools — shared drives, email, and manual tracking — that make it difficult to see the status of applications, ensure consistent decision-making, and produce timely reports for ministers (problem). This results in delayed payments to grant recipients, inconsistent assessment quality, and an inability to provide ministers with up-to-date programme data (impact). Evidence: the last ministerial report took three weeks to compile manually, and two grant payments were delayed by over a month due to lost documentation (evidence).

**Proportionate Discovery Approach:**
Given the relatively small scale (£150k budget, single team), a one-week focused discovery is appropriate:
- Day 1-2: Shadow the team, map the actual process, identify pain points
- Day 3: Review existing government grant management platforms and assess fit
- Day 4: Meet with ministerial private office to understand reporting needs precisely
- Day 5: Produce findings and options paper — the answer might be SharePoint, might be an existing platform, might be a simpler process improvement

This one week of discovery could save the programme from spending £150,000 on a SharePoint site when a £30,000 configuration of an existing grant management platform would serve better.
assessmentCriteria: Identified assumptions that go beyond the obvious technology choice
Discovery questions focus on understanding the problem and process, not gathering requirements for the stated solution
Problem statement describes the pain and impact without prescribing a solution
Discovery approach is proportionate to the scale of the request and respects the timeline

commonMistakes: Accepting a solution request at face value without exploring the underlying problem
Treating discovery as a box-ticking exercise rather than genuine learning
Allowing the loudest stakeholder to define the problem without hearing other perspectives
Spending so long in discovery that the window for delivery closes — discovery must be timeboxed
Confusing the stated problem with the real problem and designing for the wrong one
Ignoring policy intent and designing a technically correct solution that doesn't serve the policy goal
Failing to surface and test assumptions embedded in the project brief
Skipping discovery because 'we already know what we need' — the most dangerous assumption of all

weakVsStrong.weak: A weak SA receives the DESNZ policy team's request for a database and immediately begins designing the schema. They produce an entity-relationship diagram, recommend SQL Server, estimate the hosting costs, and present a delivery plan. The database is built on time and on budget. Six months later, the policy team is still spending six weeks each quarter processing data because the bottleneck was never data storage — it was data quality and manual reconciliation. The database sits largely unused while the team continues working with spreadsheets.
weakVsStrong.strong: A strong SA receives the same request and spends a week understanding the problem. They discover that the real issue is data quality and process inefficiency, not data storage. They identify that Ofgem already holds much of the needed data. They present three options to the programme board, including one that costs 40% less and addresses the actual bottleneck. The selected solution reduces the quarterly processing cycle from six weeks to two weeks — a genuine improvement in the team's ability to do their job and serve the policy goal.

workplaceSignals: You routinely ask 'what problem are we solving?' before discussing solutions, and the team expects and values this
Stakeholders come to you early in the process because they know you'll help them clarify their thinking
Your discovery outputs are concise, actionable documents that the team actually references during design
You can explain the policy intent behind the services you work on, not just the technical requirements
You've successfully reframed at least one project brief from a solution request to a problem statement
You challenge assumptions respectfully and people appreciate it rather than resenting it
Your solutions address root causes rather than symptoms, reducing the need for rework
You can point to specific examples where discovery changed the direction of a project for the better
